title: Expansion, quoting & variables
about: How bash turns a typed line into the words a command receives: quoting, escaping, variables and the environment, wildcards, brace and tilde expansion, command substitution, arithmetic and aliases.

questions.title: Stages of evaluating a command line
questions.text: Put the stages the shell applies to a command line in order.

items.why: The first word may be replaced by an alias.
Values are filled in before the file-name patterns are looked at.

items.t: Expand wildcards such as `*.txt` into file names
items.why: Done on the result of the previous stage.

items.t: Set up redirections, then run the command
items.why: The program finally starts with the final list of words.

questions.title: Who expands the star
questions.text: In `ls *.txt`, who replaces `*.txt` by a list of file names?

options.t: The shell, before `ls` starts; `ls` only sees the resulting names.
options.why: Programs do not do their own globbing.

options.t: `ls` itself, which understands the star and looks for the matching files.
The kernel, when `ls` asks it to open a file with a star in its name.
options.why: The kernel knows nothing about patterns.

options.t: The terminal emulator, before the line is handed over to the shell.

questions.title: Seeing the final words
questions.text: Which command shows exactly what arguments a command receives after all expansions, one per line?

options.t: `printf '%s\n' words...` (for example `printf '%s\n' *.txt`)
options.why: It prints each expanded word on its own line.

options.t: `echo -n words...`, which prints the words without a final newline
options.why: That only suppresses the final newline.

options.t: `type words...`, which describes how each of the words would be executed
`alias words...`, which lists the shorthands that have been defined

questions.title: Variable before glob
questions.text: `Y='*.c'; echo $Y` prints the names of the `.c` files of the directory, while `echo "$Y"` prints `*.c`. Why?

options.t: An unquoted `$Y` is expanded first, and then split into words and globbed; in double quotes neither happens.
options.why: That is why variables are normally quoted.

options.t: Because `Y` has not been exported, so `echo` cannot see that it holds a pattern.
Because double quotes delete the star from the value of the variable before the variable is used in the command.
options.why: They keep it as a literal character.

options.t: Because `echo` expands the stars it receives only when they are in single quotes.

questions.title: Quoting mechanisms
questions.text: Match each form with its behaviour.

pairs.r: Everything is literal, no expansions at all
pairs.why: Even `$` and backslash are plain characters.

pairs.r: Variables, `$(...)` and arithmetic are expanded; wildcards and word splitting are not
The next character is taken literally
pairs.why: Useful for a single special character.

pairs.r: A string where escapes like `\t` are interpreted
pairs.why: An ANSI-C style string of bash.

questions.title: Single versus double
questions.text: Given `X=world`, what does `echo 'hi $X'` print?

options.t: `hi $X`
`hi world`
`hi`
An error because `$X` is not defined.

questions.title: Double quotes
questions.text: Given `X=world`, what does `echo "hi $X"` print?

options.t: `hi world`
options.why: Double quotes still allow variable expansion.

options.t: `hi $X`
`"hi world"`
options.why: The shell removes the quotes before `echo` sees the word.

options.t: `hi X`
options.why: The dollar sign is used by the expansion.

questions.title: Quotes join text
questions.text: What does `echo '$X'"$X"` print when `X=world`?

options.t: `$Xworld`
options.why: Two adjacent quoted pieces form a single word: the first literal, the second expanded.

options.t: `$X world`
options.why: There is no space between the pieces.

options.t: `worldworld`
options.why: The first piece is not expanded.

questions.title: Whitespace and quotes
questions.text: How many arguments does `echo a   b` pass to `echo`, compared with `echo "a   b"`?

options.t: Two, and then one.
options.why: Unquoted blanks separate words; a quoted string is one word and keeps its spaces.

options.t: One and one.
Three and one.
Two and two.

questions.title: Apostrophe in text
questions.text: Which command prints `it's` correctly?

options.t: `echo "it's"`
options.why: A single quote inside double quotes is an ordinary character.

options.t: `echo 'it's'`
options.why: The quote after `it` closes the string; the rest is left open.

options.t: `echo it's`
`echo 'it\'s'`
options.why: A backslash does not escape inside single quotes.

questions.title: Backslash in quotes
questions.text: What do `echo 'a\nb'` and `echo "a\nb"` print in bash (with the default `echo`)?

options.t: Both print `a\nb` literally on one line.
options.why: Bash's `echo` does not interpret `\n` unless `-e` is used.

options.t: Both print `a` and `b` on two lines.
The first prints two lines, the second one.
options.why: Neither quoting form turns `\n` into a newline.

options.t: Both print nothing.

wrong.why: That removes the trailing newline only.

questions.title: Dollar sign as text
questions.text: Which command prints the text `$HOME` literally?

options.t: `echo '$HOME'` or `echo \$HOME`
options.why: Single quotes or a backslash prevent the expansion.

options.t: `echo "$HOME"`, because the double quotes keep the text as it is
`echo $HOME`, since `echo` prints whatever text it receives
`echo ${HOME}`, because the braces stop the expansion

questions.title: Backslash and newline
questions.text: What is the effect of a backslash at the end of a line in a script?

options.t: It removes the newline, so the command continues on the next line.
It ends the command at that point and runs whatever has been typed so far.
It comments out the next line, so that the shell ignores its contents.
It prints a literal backslash and then starts a new command on the next line.
options.why: Inside quotes or not, the pair backslash-newline is removed (except within single quotes).

questions.text: Set the variable `NAME` to `Ana`: `NAME{{0}}Ana`
questions.note: No spaces around `=` in a shell assignment.

wrong.why: Pascal-style assignment does not exist in bash.

questions.title: Spaces in an assignment
questions.text: What does `C = 3` do in bash?

options.t: It tries to run a command called `C` with the arguments `=` and `3`, and fails with "command not found".
options.why: Assignments must have no spaces around `=`.

options.t: It sets the variable `C` to the value 3, since the shell simply ignores the spaces that are written around the `=` sign.
It compares `C` with 3 and sets the exit status to 0 when they are equal.
It prints the number 3 on the screen and leaves `C` undefined.

questions.title: Using a variable
questions.text: Which command prints the value of `NAME`?

options.t: `echo $NAME` or `echo ${NAME}`
options.why: The dollar sign asks for the value.

options.t: `echo NAME`, since `echo` looks up a variable when its name is given
`echo &NAME`, where the ampersand asks for the value of the variable
options.why: An ampersand would start a background job.

options.t: `echo %NAME%`, where the percent signs surround the name of the variable

questions.title: Braces
questions.text: Why would you write `${NAME}_backup` instead of `$NAME_backup`?

options.t: Without braces the shell reads the name as `NAME_backup` (letters, digits and underscores), probably undefined.
options.why: Braces mark where the name ends.

options.t: Braces make the variable exported, so that its value is passed on to all the commands and programs that you start afterwards.
Braces make the expansion happen earlier, before the other expansions of the line.
There is no difference at all: the two forms always give exactly the same result.
options.why: The difference is exactly the name boundary.

questions.text: Match each predefined variable with its content.

pairs.why: Usually set by the login process.

questions.title: Exporting
questions.text: What is the difference between `FOO=1` and `export FOO=1`?

options.t: With `export`, the variable is passed to the child processes started afterwards; otherwise it stays in the current shell.
options.why: The environment is inherited, shell variables are not.

options.t: `export` makes the variable read-only, so it cannot be changed by later assignments.
`export` saves the variable in a file in your home directory, so that it is available again at the next login.
There is no difference: every variable is automatically passed to the child processes.
options.why: A child only sees exported variables.

questions.title: Child sees nothing
questions.text: After `FOO=local` (no export), what does `bash -c 'echo "[$FOO]"'` print?

options.why: The child shell does not inherit a variable that was not exported.

options.t: `[local]`
`[FOO]`
options.why: The value is empty, not the name.

options.t: An error about `FOO`.
options.why: An unset variable expands to an empty string.

questions.title: Temporary variable
questions.text: What does `BAR=tmp bash -c 'echo "[$BAR]"'` print, and what is `$BAR` afterwards in the current shell?

options.t: `[tmp]`; afterwards `$BAR` is unchanged (empty if it was unset).
options.why: A prefix assignment lives only for that command's environment.

options.t: `[]`, and afterwards `BAR` stays set to `tmp` in the current shell.
`[tmp]`, and afterwards `BAR` remains set to `tmp` in the current shell.
An error, because assignments cannot be written in front of a command.

questions.title: Changes in a subshell
questions.text: After `X=outer; (X=inner; echo $X); echo $X`, what is printed?

options.t: `inner`, then `outer`
options.why: The parentheses create a subshell; its changes are lost when it ends.

options.t: `inner` then `inner`
`outer` then `outer`
options.why: Inside the subshell the new value is used.

options.t: An error, since variables cannot be redefined.

questions.title: printenv versus echo
questions.text: You ran `FOO=x` (no export). What do `echo $FOO` and `printenv FOO` show?

options.t: `x` for the first; nothing for the second, because `printenv` shows only exported variables.
options.why: A quick test for whether a variable is exported.

options.t: `x` for both commands, since `printenv` also reads the variables of the shell.
options.why: `printenv` reads the environment, not shell variables.

options.t: Nothing for both commands, because a variable that has not been exported is not visible to either of them.
options.why: The shell variable has a value.

options.t: An error for the first command, because the variable is not in the environment.

questions.title: Modifying PATH
questions.text: Which line adds `~/bin` to the end of the command search path for this session and its children?

options.t: `export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin"`
options.why: Keeps the old value and appends the new directory.

options.t: `PATH=$HOME/bin`
options.why: Replaces the whole search path, so `ls` is no longer found.

options.t: `export PATH=$PATH:~/bin &`, which puts the assignment in the background where it has no effect
options.why: The `&` runs the assignment in a background subshell, which has no effect on your shell.

options.t: `cd ~/bin`

questions.title: Breaking PATH
questions.text: After `PATH=/nonexistent`, which commands still work?

options.t: `/bin/ls`
options.why: A word with a slash is used as a path; no `PATH` search is needed.

options.t: `cd /tmp`
options.why: Builtins are part of the shell and never consult `PATH`.

options.t: `ls`
options.why: It is searched in `PATH`, which no longer lists its directory.

options.t: `cat`
options.why: Also an external program searched in `PATH`.

options.t: `grep root /etc/passwd`

questions.title: Order of search in PATH
questions.text: `PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin` and both directories contain `tool`. Which one runs?

options.t: The one in `/usr/local/bin`: directories are searched from left to right and the first match wins.
options.why: That is how you can override a system program.

options.t: The one in `/usr/bin`, because bash searches the directories of `PATH` from right to left and stops at the first match.
Both of them, one after the other, and the output of each is printed.
Neither, until bash asks which of the two programs you really want to run.

questions.title: Hidden files and star
questions.text: Does `ls *.dat` list a file named `.hid.dat`?

options.t: No: a leading dot must be matched explicitly, so `*` does not match hidden files.
Yes, because `*` matches every possible name, hidden ones included.
Yes, but it prints a warning that the file is hidden, together with its name.
options.why: It is not listed at all.

options.t: Only when the command is run by root, who is allowed to see hidden files.

questions.text: In a directory with no `.nomatch` files, what does `echo *.nomatch` print by default?

options.t: `*.nomatch`
options.why: A pattern with no match is left as it is (unless the `nullglob` option is set).

options.t: An empty line.
An error message.

The list of `.dat` files.
Nothing.

questions.title: Names with spaces
questions.text: A directory has `sp ace.dat`. Why might `rm *.dat` still work correctly even though the name has a space?

options.t: A glob yields one word per matching file, so the space does not split the name; the problem is with *unquoted variables*.
options.why: The safe habit is `rm -- *.dat` and always quoting variables.

options.t: Because `rm` itself knows how to handle spaces in the names it is given.
options.why: `rm` receives a separate argument for each name.

options.t: Because the shell adds quotes around every name in the output of the expansion, which keeps the spaces inside each name.
It does not work; the command fails on the file with a space in its name.

questions.title: Brace expansion
questions.text: Match each brace expression with its expansion.

extras.r: every file that matches a or b
extras.why: Braces do not look at the file system.

questions.title: Brace versus glob
questions.text: What is the difference between `echo {a,b}.dat` and `echo [ab].dat`?

options.t: The brace version always prints `a.dat b.dat`, whether the files exist or not; the glob prints only existing matches.
They are equivalent, and both print only the files that exist in the directory.
The glob always prints both names, even if one of the files does not exist.
The brace version needs the files to exist, since it looks them up in the directory before it prints their names.
options.why: It does not look at the file system.

questions.title: Handy brace use
questions.text: Which command creates a backup copy of `config.ini` as `config.ini.bak` with the least typing?

options.t: `cp config.ini{,.bak}`
`cp config.ini[.bak]`
options.why: A bracket would match one character.

options.t: `cp config.ini*.bak`
`cp {config.ini}.bak`
options.why: A single item in braces does not expand.

questions.title: Tilde
questions.text: What does `echo ~root` print, and what does `echo "~root"` print?

options.t: `/root` and then `~root`
options.why: The tilde is expanded only when unquoted.

options.t: `/root` both times.
`~root` both times.
The current user's home in both cases.

questions.title: Command substitution
questions.text: What does `echo "Today: $(date +%F)"` do?

options.t: It runs `date +%F` first and puts its output into the string.
options.why: The command inside `$(...)` is replaced by what it prints.

options.t: It prints the text `$(date +%F)` literally, since it is inside double quotes.
options.why: That would be the result with single quotes.

options.t: It runs `echo` twice, once for the text and once for the date command.
It stores the date in a variable called `Today` and prints nothing.

questions.title: Backticks
questions.text: How do `` `cmd` `` and `$(cmd)` differ?

options.t: They do the same, but `$(...)` nests more easily and is more readable.
options.why: The backtick form is the older syntax.

options.t: Backticks run the command in the background, while `$(...)` waits for it to end.
`$(...)` only works inside scripts, while backticks also work at the prompt.
Backticks print the command instead of running it, which is how you debug.

questions.title: Trailing newlines
questions.text: What happens to the newlines at the end of a command's output in `$(cmd)`?

options.t: They are removed from the end; newlines inside the output remain (when it is quoted).
options.why: So `X=$(date)` does not keep a final newline.

options.t: All the newlines are preserved, including those at the very end of the output, so that the value always ends with a line break.
All the newlines are removed, even those in the middle of the output.
options.why: Only trailing ones, unless the expansion is unquoted and word splitting joins lines with spaces.

options.t: They are replaced by the two characters `\n`, so the text stays on one line.
options.why: Literal backslash sequences are not created.

questions.title: Lines in substitution
questions.text: `echo "$(echo a; echo b)" | wc -l` prints 2, while `echo $(echo a; echo b) | wc -l` prints 1. Why?

options.t: Unquoted, the result is split into words that `echo` joins with spaces; quoted, the newline is kept.
Because `wc` counts the quotes as if they were line separators in the text.
Because the second form does not run the first `echo`, so a line is missing.
Because quoting changes what the inner `echo` prints to the pipe, and not the way the outer command receives it.
options.why: It changes how the outer command receives it.

questions.title: Counting with substitution
questions.text: Which command stores the number of entries of the current directory in `N`?

options.t: `N=$(ls | wc -l)`
options.why: The output of the pipeline is captured.

options.t: `N=ls | wc -l`
options.why: That is a pipeline: the assignment runs in its own subshell and is lost, and `wc -l` just waits for keyboard input.

options.t: `ls | wc -l > N`
options.why: Writes the number into a file called `N`.

options.t: `N="ls | wc -l"`
options.why: Stores the text of the command.

questions.title: What an alias is
questions.text: What is an alias?

options.t: A shorthand that the shell substitutes for the first word of a command, such as `alias ll='ls -l'`.
options.why: It is text replacement done early in the evaluation.

options.t: A second name for a file on the disk, which points to the same data as the first name, as a hard link does.
A variable that can be exported to the child processes of the shell.
A stored script that the shell runs automatically each time you log in.

questions.title: Keeping an alias
questions.text: You defined `alias rm='rm -i'` in a terminal. When will it be available again after you close the terminal?

options.t: Only if the definition is written to `~/.bashrc` (or another startup file).
options.why: Aliases live in the shell's memory.

options.t: Always, because aliases are stored on the disk as soon as they are defined.
Only in the terminals that were already open when the alias was defined.
options.why: New ones will not have it either.

options.t: Only for the root user, since aliases are stored in the system configuration.

questions.title: Bypassing an alias

options.why: A quoted or escaped first word is not alias-expanded.

options.why: `rm` has no such option: aliases are expanded by the shell before `rm` even starts.

options.t: `unalias`, which runs the real command for a single line
options.why: Needs a name, and removes the alias for the session.

options.t: `rm! file`, where the exclamation mark bypasses aliases

questions.title: Alias and scripts

options.t: Non-interactive shells running scripts do not expand aliases by default (and do not read `~/.bashrc`).
options.why: Use functions or full commands in scripts.

options.t: Because aliases only work for the root user and scripts run as an ordinary user.
Because scripts cannot use commands such as `ls`, which are reserved for the interactive shell and not allowed in files.
Because aliases are deleted as soon as `chmod +x` is run on the script file.
